title: Speed Cameras Spread to More States, and Drivers Are Fighting Back
summary:
If you've driven through a school zone in Florida lately, you may have noticed the new speed cameras. Carlos Acosta certainly did—he got two tickets. "I think it's a money grab," he said. "That's what irks me the most. It's all about making money."

Acosta is not alone. Millions of drivers across the country are encountering automated speed cameras for the first time, and a growing backlash is brewing. Florida recently joined more than two dozen states that allow speed cameras, including California, Hawaii, Michigan, and Minnesota. Safety advocates say the cameras are effective: they force drivers to slow down, reducing crashes and fatalities.

"The whole point of the cameras is reducing the speeds, which leads to crashes at lower speeds when they happen, so there's fewer people dying," said Raul Avelar, an engineer with the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

But critics argue the cameras are more about revenue than safety. Ted Hollander, a lawyer at The Ticket Clinic, points out that many tickets are issued during school hours when children are inside. "We don't really think it's truly about safety, because if it was, it would only be during the times when the kids are around," he said. "We feel like it's an illegal tax."

The backlash has found an ally in the Trump administration. Last month, the Federal Highway Administration quietly removed speed cameras from its list of "Proven Safety Countermeasures," a move that alarmed safety advocates. The agency said the change was part of a broader review to align with administration priorities.

Supporters of speed cameras insist they are not a cash grab. Rep. Laura Friedman, a California Democrat who authored the state's speed camera law, said, "We have so many safeguards built into this to make sure it is purely a traffic calming and speed reduction effort." The real test will come in Los Angeles, where speed cameras are set to go live in the coming months—in a city famous for its car culture and fast drivers.
why_it_matters: This fight is about more than tickets: it tests whether automated enforcement can be trusted as a public-safety tool when many citizens see it as government surveillance and taxation. The outcome in states like Florida and cities like Los Angeles could shape how new road-safety technology is adopted nationwide.

background_read: Speed cameras are automated devices that photograph a vehicle and its license plate when it exceeds the posted limit, then mail a citation to the registered owner.

The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (a nonprofit research organization funded by the insurance industry) has long argued that lower speeds reduce crash deaths, which is why its engineer Raul Avelar supports the cameras.

The Federal Highway Administration (the federal agency that sets road-safety guidance for states) had included automated enforcement on its list of 'Proven Safety Countermeasures' until last month, when the Trump administration removed it.
The Ticket Clinic (a private law firm that specializes in fighting traffic tickets) represents drivers who see the cameras as an 'illegal tax' rather than a safety tool.
Los Angeles, where cameras will launch soon, is known for both sprawling freeways and a strong car culture, making it a key test of whether automated enforcement can work in a car-dependent region.

perspectives.description: Safety researchers argue that slower vehicles cause fewer deadly crashes, and automated cameras can change driver behavior around schools. From this view, the cameras are a proven countermeasure that protects both drivers and pedestrians.

Drivers like Carlos Acosta see the tickets as a 'money grab,' especially when cameras issue citations outside school hours. Critics worry that local governments will use automated fines as an illegal tax rather than a genuine safety program.

The dispute highlights a deeper tension between evidence-based safety policy and public acceptance. Automated enforcement can reduce fatalities, but it also raises questions about due process, transparency, and whether revenue motives undermine trust.

The Los Angeles rollout will be a closely watched test. If cities add clear safeguards—such as using cameras only during active school hours—public opinion may shift, but if distrust grows, more states could follow the federal government's lead and reject automated enforcement.
